overview: The atlas colors a large part of Madagascar “Vazimba” from 600 to 800, but that neat shape is not evidence for a centralized state, one ethnicity, or a surveyed border. A modern French-Malagasy research project instead investigates thirteenth- to nineteenth-century burials while testing later stories of conquest, coexistence, and mixing. Those much later questions cannot identify a seventh-century population. The earliest securely relevant archaeology documents communities in Madagascar without telling us that they called themselves Vazimba. Seventh- and eighth-century northeastern villages provide settlement evidence, although first-arrival arguments remain contested. The decoded atlas feature is one identical 121-position polygon in the 600 and 700 snapshots. It excludes Vohémar and Ampasimahavelona, where much of the period evidence was excavated, so the card distinguishes island history from the painted footprint. Pottery, shell and fish remains, stone tools, and settlement traces reveal real work and ingenuity. Direct evidence for kinship, children’s teaching, medicine, toilets, and writing is absent. At 800 the map relabels sampled interior points “Malagasy”; it records a software seam, not a conquest, extinction, or sudden replacement.

periods.title: An atlas band begins, not a kingdom
periods.summary: The 600 snapshot introduces one polygon labeled Vazimba. No contemporary document names a ruler, capital, army, tax system, or border. This first band is an editorial guide across a poorly dated interval. The map cannot turn later ancestral traditions into a securely attested seventh-century state.

periods.title: Language models offer a range, not a landing day
periods.summary: One lexical-distance model places Malagasy dialect divergence between 623 and 681 CE. Its authors present a quantitative linguistic estimate, not an excavated voyage or a Vazimba founding date. Spoken language can preserve relationships across oceans, but a modelled interval cannot identify one ship, village, or named community.

periods.title: Mixed origins resist a single-founder story
periods.summary: Linguistic comparison connects Malagasy most strongly with Southeast Barito languages while also detecting Malay, Javanese, and Bantu layers. Those contacts imply movement and interaction across the Indian Ocean. They do not establish that every person present from 650 to 675 shared one origin, label, or political allegiance.

periods.title: Stone tools complicate a tidy arrival tale
periods.summary: Northern rock-shelter evidence includes small stone tools and disputed early dates, while associated food remains are missing. Researchers emphasize how little is known about the users’ way of life. This band therefore records an archaeological question, not a claim that the toolmakers were Vazimba or lived everywhere inside the polygon.

periods.title: The painted shape stays exactly the same
periods.summary: The atlas redraws the same 121-position polygon at 700 and changes only its stored interval to 700 through 800. Representative ownership and geometry remain unchanged. That digital continuity does not demonstrate two centuries of fixed borders; it shows that one basemap outline was reused.

periods.title: Estuarine settlement becomes archaeologically visible
periods.summary: Survey in the Vohémar region identified early estuarine villages dating to the seventh and eighth centuries. Archaeological phases and material scatters reveal settlement without supplying a contemporary ethnic name. The sites are valuable evidence for Madagascar in this band, even though the atlas polygon excludes their northeastern coast.

periods.title: Crop silence is useful evidence
periods.summary: Eighth-century deposits at Ampasimahavelona yielded local ceramics and wild fauna but no crop remains in the archaeobotanical samples. The study warns that early agriculture may still be archaeologically invisible. It is safer to report the zero than to serve an imaginary bowl of rice to every household.

periods.title: The endpoint changes a label, not the people
periods.summary: At 800 the exact Vazimba feature disappears and interior probes receive a broad “malagasy” owner. Archaeological reviews separate early settlement and trade from much later kingdom formation. No evidence ties this file boundary to defeat, evacuation, or biological replacement, so continuity is the responsible ending.

sections.title: Read the label before believing the border

items.text: The imported index dates Vazimba approximately 600 to 800, while coverage classifies it as a state because that is the inherited database kind. Neither field supplies institutions. The researched override uses “culture” and an atlas-layer name so interface grammar does not silently manufacture a kingdom.

The imported summary repeats popular first-inhabitant and short-stature stories, then presents scholarly speculation as though it identified a population. Later scholarship finds multiple meanings and no secure target-period body type. This card excludes the dwarf or pygmy trope instead of turning a contested tradition into anatomy.

Both target snapshots decode to one Polygon with one ring, 121 stored positions, and the same geometry hash. Its box spans roughly 43.29° to 50.50° east and 25.66° to 12.27° south. No direct arc seam or sampled ownership overlap appears.

Antananarivo, Fianarantsoa, Manakara, Marovoay, Bemaraha, Ranomafana, and Tôlanaro test inside the shape. Toamasina, Mahajanga, Antsiranana, Toliara, Morondava, Vohémar, and Nosy Be test outside. A polygon missing major coasts and the key excavated region cannot be a national or ethnic frontier.

Across all 50 border snapshots, the exact id occurs only at 600 and 700. At 500 the sampled interior points have no owner; at 800 they become “malagasy.” The changing owner strings describe the atlas editor’s categories. They do not identify what residents called themselves.

sections.title: Use archaeology without assigning an ancient name

items.text: A chronology project assembled 278 age determinations for late prehistoric Madagascar, underscoring how settlement dates must be evaluated as a body rather than selected one by one. The wide debate blocks the simple claim that a named Vazimba people first arrived precisely in 600.

The Vohémar-region sequence identifies early estuarine villages of the seventh and eighth centuries and an Ampasimahavelona phase continuing into the tenth. These are archaeological phases defined by sites and materials. The excavators do not supply a contemporary ethnic label, so “Vazimba village” would overstate the evidence.

Vohémar survey found pottery and shell scatters marking villages and hamlets, including settlements dated to the eighth century. Their date and contents make the region unusually useful for this interval, yet Vohémar falls outside the atlas shape. The evidence belongs to early Madagascar history, not every colored point.

Ambohiposa yielded tiny stone tools, while acidic deposits destroyed associated animal bones. Project archaeologists later searched for comparable sites with better preservation. Stone flakes can show skilled action; they cannot announce a personal name, language, family structure, complete diet, or Vazimba identity.

A Malagasy archaeologist’s handbook chapter separates initial settlement, late-first-millennium exchange, urban growth, and later kingdoms. Keeping those stages apart prevents a common shortcut: projecting the centralized polities known from later centuries backward onto very sparse seventh- and eighth-century settlement evidence.

sections.title: Put only evidenced food on the table

items.text: Terebralia mangrove shell, conch, and a fish spine occur in well-contexted Ampasimahavelona deposits. They show that people gathered and processed estuarine or marine foods. The assemblage does not provide a complete menu, meal order, recipe, or proof that every early Malagasy settlement ate alike.

The sampled eighth-century Ampasimahavelona deposits produced zero crop remains. Researchers explicitly allow that farming may have escaped detection, but absence still matters. Rice, mung bean, and cotton evidence in the same study comes from other places or later contexts, so it cannot be moved backward for a tastier story.

Directly dated introduced sheep and zebu in the reviewed faunal record are younger than about 1020 calibrated years before present, roughly 890 to 990 CE. That is after this card ends. A zebu-centered 600-to-800 Vazimba economy would therefore outrun the current direct dates.

Directly dated sheep and zebu remain later than this card, while earlier deposits preserve only partial food evidence. Archaeological silence is not proof of fasting; organic scraps often disappear. It does mean researchers cannot securely reconstruct roasting, boiling, portion sharing, leftovers, or livestock meals for every household.

Later genetics reveals ancestry connected with African and Southeast Asian populations, while language records similarly layered contacts. Neither evidence type is a grocery list. Bananas, taro, rice, cattle, and culinary roles need their own dated evidence, so attractive migration “packages” are kept outside the target-period menu.

sections.title: See pots, stone, and exchange without inventing workshops

items.text: Coarse oxidized basins and hole-mouth jar rims define part of the Ampasimahavelona ceramic tradition. Their repeated forms demonstrate clay-working knowledge and vessels made for use. A sherd is wonderfully chatty about technique, but it does not identify the potter’s age, gender, household, teacher, or spoken name.

A peer-reviewed archaeobotanical study combines plant remains with archaeological distributions to investigate Indian Ocean movement. That breadth reveals connected histories while discouraging a royal-trade shortcut. Sparse early objects and later crops do not make the entire island urban or identify every voyager as Vazimba.

Madagascar’s archaeological sequence includes worked stone alongside ceramics and later imported goods. Manufacturing any repeated form required material selection and controlled action. Because food, structures, and workshops preserve unevenly, artifacts support practical skill more securely than a detailed scene assigning benches, specialists, apprentices, or production quotas.

Comparative linguistics finds Malagasy shaped by a Southeast Barito base plus Malay, Javanese, Bantu, and other contacts. Words can preserve old encounters, including maritime ones, without providing a shipping manifest. Linguistic layers support connected histories, but they cannot assign a particular seventh-century pot to a speaker.

Genomic modelling links much present Malagasy Asian ancestry most closely with Banjar-related populations shaped by earlier Malay contact. The authors warn that estimated admixture dates describe mixing processes rather than first arrival. The result supports complex voyaging histories, not one fleet, captain, cargo, or Vazimba dynasty.

At Ampasimahavelona, artifact scatter runs along a river terrace and old estuary. Excavators suggest the settlement may have been linear, perhaps with houses facing the river. Both “may” and “perhaps” matter: no secure wall plan lets us specify stilts, timber species, roofs, rooms, or sleeping places.

The atlas shape excludes Vohémar even though that northeastern region supplies the interval’s clearest village evidence. This mismatch is a useful lesson: map coverage and archaeological coverage answer different questions. The first is an imported visualization; the second comes from excavated contexts, dates, artifacts, and explicit uncertainty.

A Nosy Be sediment record suggests intensified human effects around 1300 calibrated years before present, approximately the late seventh or eighth century. Yet related ceramics and food remains lack direct dates. Environmental change can guide questions, but it cannot by itself identify settlers or their exact activities.

Northern lake sediments show major drought and fire signals beginning mainly about 1100 years ago, after this atlas layer. Researchers separate climate stress from human burning. The result warns against blaming people in 600 to 800 for every later forest change or imagining an untouched environment before one dramatic event.

No excavated target-period house in these sources preserves a complete domestic interior. Pottery and food refuse show activities, and settlement locations suggest spatial choices, but beds, doors, cooking corners, private rooms, and household size remain unknown. A careful reconstruction leaves those rooms unfurnished.

sections.title: Keep families and social identities open

items.text: Later texts and traditions use Vazimba in several ways: earlier inhabitants, former rulers, sacred dead, or ancestral powers. Rajoelinoro warns of temporal dilation and anachronism in oral accounts. These meanings deserve respect and study, but they cannot label every family living on Madagascar between 600 and 800.

The MadInter and MAFMAD projects are using burials and biomolecular methods to investigate mobility, family structure, and kinship in much later contexts. If those questions still require new analysis, this card cannot confidently supply seventh-century marriage rules, descent groups, residence patterns, or inheritance.

Present Malagasy genomes show heterogeneous mixtures of African and Asian ancestry, with regional and sex-biased patterns. The researchers explicitly say ancient DNA is needed to test possible earlier populations. Modern genetic clusters therefore cannot be renamed “Vazimba families” or projected unchanged across twelve centuries.

Mikea communities have sometimes been recruited into stories about unchanged first inhabitants. Genome-wide analysis instead found sampled Mikea broadly similar in ancestry to other sampled Malagasy groups and interpreted foraging as cultural reversion. Modern subsistence cannot serve as a biological time capsule for the atlas label.

Dewar and Wright’s archaeological review catalogs ceramics, stone artifacts, settlements, subsistence, and exchange. Its target-period evidence does not identify which tasks belonged to women, men, elders, children, specialists, or guests. This card therefore describes material activities without assigning unsupported gender or age roles.

sections.title: Let children learn, while admitting what is missing

items.text: Adelaar’s research record identifies a 1603 European wordbook and seventeenth-century Sorabe texts as the earliest systematically studied Malagasy materials. It supplies no written classroom evidence from 600 to 800: no lesson text, exercise, pupil name, or school record. Learning occurred, but this source cannot say where or how.

Malagasy is an Austronesian language with important African and Asian contact layers and many regional varieties. That linguistic history shows generations successfully transmitted speech. It does not recover a lesson spoken in 700, identify its teacher, or prove that the people represented by the atlas used one uniform dialect.

A dialect-distance model estimates a central divergence window of 623 to 681 CE. The authors present a statistical reconstruction from modern vocabularies, not a classroom transcript. It is informative about language history while remaining too indirect to date one settlement, migration, or child’s first words.

The earliest systematically studied Malagasy materials are a 1603 European wordbook and seventeenth-century Sorabe texts. That leaves no secure written sample from 600 to 800. Spoken knowledge may have flourished, but this card will not counterfeit an early inscription simply because writing looks impressive.

Modern written sample: “Ny teny malagasy no tenim-pirenena.” The official French counterpart says “Le malgache est la langue nationale,” translated here as “Malagasy is the national language.” This 1992 Latin-script sentence needs no transliteration. It demonstrates living written Malagasy, not Vazimba wording from the atlas interval.

sections.title: Treat health and care as an evidence gap

items.text: Heiske and colleagues review modern population history and genetics; their study does not document a 600-to-800 healer, medicinal plant, surgical tool, diagnosis, birth practice, or caregiving arrangement. Population ancestry cannot fill that medical record. Within this card, target-period treatment and care therefore remain undetermined.

MadInter’s funerary research works with collective burials dating centuries after this interval. That program shows what direct health and kinship research can require: bodies, contexts, dates, and laboratory evidence. It does not retroactively diagnose people represented by the 600 and 700 atlas polygons.

A modern genomic study found selection involving the Duffy blood-group region during the last millennium, relevant to disease biology. Genes are not prescriptions or clinic notes. The result cannot identify target-period treatments, carers, symptoms, survival rates, or a specifically Vazimba medical system.

Present-population genetic reviews repeatedly warn that ancestry estimates concern ancestors of sampled people, not necessarily the island’s first residents. Health differences likewise cannot be assigned to a legendary category without ancient individuals. “Vazimba medicine” would require dated cultural evidence that the cited research does not provide.

MadInter’s much later collective-burial program investigates biological profiles and kin relationships. Because its studied burials date to the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries, it cannot supply pregnancy care, infant feeding, disability support, or elder care for 600 to 800. That chronological limit is not evidence that people lacked care.

sections.title: Ask practical questions about water, waste, and toilets

items.text: Ampasimahavelona stood on a river terrace beside an old estuary, a location that connected settlement with aquatic resources and travel. The excavation summary does not identify a well, cistern, pipe, or household water container. Proximity to water is evidence; a reconstructed plumbing system is not.

Pottery and shell scatters mark early villages and hamlets in the Vohémar survey. Such refuse is useful evidence, but it is not automatically a toilet, sewer, or planned sanitation system. No cited target-period latrine has been securely identified, so bathroom architecture remains an explicit gap.

Radimilahy’s archaeological handbook review does not report a secure 600-to-800 drain, cesspit, sewer, bathing room, or dedicated toilet. That source silence cannot tell us where every person relieved themselves. It does allow one child-friendly conclusion: archaeologists sometimes learn from ancient trash, but trash and toilets are different categories.

Crowther and colleagues associate rice from Mahilaka with deposits dated about 1050 to 1350 and cite irrigation there by roughly 1100. Both lie centuries after this card. They demonstrate later water management, not a pipe, canal, or paddy system that can be moved into 600 to 800.

Virah-Sawmy and colleagues’ lake-sediment record tracks drought, fire, vegetation, and human impact mainly after this interval. That environmental archive does not report drinking-water treatment, handwashing, waste rules, or seasonal sanitation for 600-to-800 residents. Those everyday practices remain unknown rather than automatically “primitive.”

Establishing estuarine settlements, making durable pottery, gathering shell, fishing, and navigating connected coasts required accumulated ecological and technical knowledge. These are substantial achievements even without a palace or king list. The evidence honors work people actually did instead of awarding them an invented centralized state.

Foundational archaeological synthesis organized Madagascar’s evidence into changing settlement, subsistence, ceramic, and exchange phases. That is an achievement of method: discovery includes comparing contexts rather than collecting exciting objects alone. Even a revised timeline cannot identify toolmakers as Vazimba merely because the atlas needs a label.

The crop study’s most useful eighth-century result is partly negative: no crops were recovered at Ampasimahavelona. By publishing zeros and separating later rice and cotton, researchers made absence informative. Scientific restraint is an achievement too, especially when a more colorful story would be easier to tell.

Modern genetics reveals complex African and Southeast Asian ancestry rather than a pure founder population. The authors caution that mixing dates do not equal first arrival dates. That complexity fits an ocean-crossing history of encounters, while refusing the racial myth that one modern group preserves an untouched Vazimba genome.

At the atlas endpoint, sampled interior points change from “vazimba” to “malagasy” without a mapped battle or evacuation. Later traditions continue using Vazimba in historical and sacred senses. The careful conclusion is continuity and transformation: a software category ends, while Malagasy communities and contested ancestral meanings continue.

ending.text: The atlas’s Vazimba polygon ends at 800 because its next file uses a broader “malagasy” label. No cited source describes a conquest, collective death, forced evacuation, or state collapse at that date. Archaeology instead shows settlement and exchange continuing and becoming more visible in later centuries. The word Vazimba also continued on a different historical track. Later oral histories, sacred geographies, and written discussions used it for earlier inhabitants, former rulers, ancestors, or powerful spirits, sometimes in mutually inconsistent ways. Those traditions are evidence for how Malagasy communities remembered and organized relationships with the past; they are not a seventh-century census. Current research treats conquest, coexistence, kinship, mobility, and mixing as questions to test through excavation, isotopes, and ancient biomolecules. The ending is therefore continuity with uncertainty. People on Madagascar kept forming families, speaking, making, eating, travelling, remembering, and changing after 800. Modern Malagasy communities are living communities, not museum stand-ins for a supposedly unchanged Vazimba population, and no group should be assigned a “Vazimba genome” from the atlas color.
